causalMechanism.primaryVector: Neuroendocrine-to-myocardial sequence: post-traumatic stress disorder is characterized by sustained sympathetic overactivity with elevated circulating catecholamines, blunted vagal tone, and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis dysregulation, which leaves the myocardium primed for an exaggerated response to an acute stressor. During such an episode, a catecholamine surge acts on apical myocardial beta-receptors and produces a signaling switch from Gs to Gi-mediated pathways, together with microvascular spasm, calcium-handling disturbance, and acute energy failure from supraphysiologic fatty-acid loading; the result is apical akinesis with basal hyperkinesis — the classic takotsubo pattern — in the absence of obstructive coronary disease. The dysfunction resolves in most patients within days to weeks, but a minority have persistent ventricular impairment, and recurrence occurs in a clinically meaningful proportion, which is the basis on which a chronic disability may be claimed. Nayeri et al. (PMID 29544664) reviewed psychiatric illness in takotsubo cardiomyopathy and concluded that there is a strong association between pre-existing psychiatric illness, particularly anxiety and mood spectrum disorders, and takotsubo cardiomyopathy. Lazzeroni et al. (PMID 29168538) compared 58 takotsubo patients with and without pre-existing anxiety disorders and found that a substantial share (31 of 58) had a prior history of anxiety disorders, with the exclusively emotional stressful event rate higher in patients with anxiety disorders. Gonuguntla et al. (PMID 38331372) analyzed the National Inpatient Sample and Nationwide Readmissions Database for 2016 through 2018 and found psychiatric disorders documented in up to 43 percent of takotsubo patients, while examining whether psychiatric comorbidity altered outcomes. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory, in which the service-connected post-traumatic stress disorder is asserted to have produced a discrete cardiac disease, stress cardiomyopathy, with its own diagnostic code at DC 7020 rather than being folded into the psychiatric evaluation. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory, because the literature describes a new acute cardiac event in a previously unaffected ventricle rather than measurable worsening of an existing structural heart disease; aggravation would govern only where the record documents pre-existing cardiomyopathy or coronary disease and the claim is that the stress-mediated episodes worsened a baseline ventricular dysfunction, in which case the attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of that pre-existing disease and § 3.310(b) applies. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require: the diagnosed post-traumatic stress disorder with its documented stressor; an acute coronary syndrome evaluation that excluded obstructive coronary disease; imaging documentation of the characteristic apical ballooning pattern with reduced ejection fraction; a documented emotional or psychological trigger temporally proximate to the episode; and, for a compensable rating, serial echocardiographic evidence of persistent or recurrent left ventricular dysfunction. Only then can an examiner state that the takotsubo cardiomyopathy and any residual dysfunction are at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected post-traumatic stress disorder — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Two candid limitations must be disclosed. First, the cited literature concerns psychiatric illness broadly — principally anxiety and mood spectrum disorders — and PTSD-specific data are comparatively limited, so the association cannot be treated as PTSD-specific without individual evidence linking the episodes to PTSD symptoms. Second, takotsubo cardiomyopathy is characteristically transient, so a claim that rests only on a resolved acute episode will fail for lack of residual disability rather than for lack of causation. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include acute coronary syndrome and spontaneous coronary artery dissection, pheochromocytoma and other catecholamine-secreting tumors, sepsis and critical illness, subarachnoid hemorrhage and other acute intracranial events, thyrotoxicosis, cocaine and stimulant use, alcohol withdrawal, perioperative stress, and chemotherapy including fluoropyrimidines and checkpoint inhibitors. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating discipline under § 4.14: a cardiac rating under DC 7020 may not be combined with a second evaluation for the same heart failure symptoms under another heart code, and the psychiatric rating under § 4.130 must not be used to compensate the same limitation of daily functioning that the cardiac evaluation represents.

Primary condition: Service-connected post-traumatic stress disorder, with a documented stressor and ongoing symptom severity
Primary diagnostic-code proposal: 38 CFR § 4.130, DC 9411 (posttraumatic stress disorder), rated under the General Rating Formula for Mental Disorders at 0, 10, 30, 50, 70, or 100 percent
Secondary condition: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (stress-induced cardiomyopathy with residual or recurrent left ventricular dysfunction) in a veteran with service-connected post-traumatic stress disorder
Secondary diagnostic-code proposal: 38 CFR § 4.104, DC 7020 (cardiomyopathy) — evaluated under the General Rating Formula for Diseases of the Heart, which assigns 100 percent when a workload of 3.0 METs or less produces heart failure symptoms, 60 percent at 3.1 to 5.0 METs, 30 percent at 5.1 to 7.0 METs or with echocardiographic evidence of cardiac hypertrophy or dilatation, and 10 percent at 7.1 to 10.0 METs or when continuous medication is required for control. Qualified-human rating review required; because stress cardiomyopathy is typically reversible, a compensable evaluation depends on documented persistent or recurrent ventricular dysfunction rather than on the acute episode alone
Original nexus theory: Causation

Legal boundary: § 3.310(a) concerns proximate causation; § 3.310(b) concerns attributable worsening beyond natural progression against a qualifying baseline. The at least as likely as not standard requires individual evidence and competing causes to be weighed. Apply claim-period rating criteria and § 4.14 nonpyramiding.
